'''''Ziziphus mauritiana''''', also known as '''Indian jujube''',<ref name = "HORT"/> '''Indian plum''',<ref name = "HORT"/> '''Chinese apple'''<!--This is not a typo-->,<ref name = "Chinee">{{cite web |title=Chinese Apple |publisher=The State of Queensland, Department of Primary Industries |url=https://www.publications.qld.gov.au/ckan-publications-attachments-prod/resources/8b50de66-f425-4df4-b901-f8f692783717/chinee-apple.pdf?ETag=4f069883face2cf46f8b982248387db5 |access-date=2025-11-20}}</ref> '''ber''' ({{langx|hi|बेर}})<ref name = "HORT"/> and '''dunks''',<ref name = "HORT"/> is a [[tropical]], spiny, [[evergreen]] [[shrub]] or small tree in the buckthorn family [[Rhamnaceae]]. It is often confused with the closely related [[jujube|Chinese jujube]] (''Z. jujuba''): ''Z. mauritiana'' is common is tropical and subtropical climates, while ''Z. jujuba'' prefers temperate climates.<ref>{{cite web |title=Datasheet: Ziziphus mauritiana (jujube) |first=N |last=Pasiecznik |date=2007-08-15 |website=[[Centre for Agriculture and Bioscience International|CABI Compendium]] |url=https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/57556 |access-date=2021-10-11}}</ref>

The plant grows vigorously up to {{convert|12|m|ft}} high, with a trunk {{convert|30|cm|in}} or more in diameter. It has a spreading [[Crown (botany)|crown]] with [[Stipule|stipular]] spines and drooping branches. The fruit is oval, [[obovate]], oblong or round, and can be {{convert|2.5|-|6|cm|in}} long depending on the variety, having smooth, light green skin when unripe, turning yellow and then reddish brown as it ripens.

==Origin and Distribution==
The species is believed to be native to [[South Asia]], southern [[China]], [[Southeast Asia]], and [[Central Africa|Central]] and [[West Africa]]. It has been introduced to the tropical regions of the [[Americas]], and is now widely naturalised throughout the [[Old World]] tropics from [[Southern Africa]] through the [[Middle East]] to [[South Asia]] and [[China]], into [[Australasia]] and the [[Pacific Islands]].<ref name="PIER">{{cite web |title=Ziziphus mauritiana |website=[[Pacific Island Ecosystems at Risk]] |date=2008-01-15 |url=http://www.hear.org/pier/species/ziziphus_mauritiana.htm |access-date=2009-07-17}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |author=<!-- not stated --> |title=''Ziziphus mauritiana'' Lam. |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:719349-1 |website=powo.science.kew.org |access-date=2025-11-20}}</ref><ref name ="jules">{{cite book |editor1-last=Janick |editor1-first=Jules |editor2-last=Paull |editor2-first=Robert E. |title= The encyclopedia of fruit & nuts |publisher=[[Centre for Agriculture and Bioscience International#Publishing|CABI Publishing]] |date=March 2008 |pages= 617–619 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cjHCoMQNkcgC&q=Indian%20Jujube%20nutritional%20value&pg=PA617 |access-date=2009-07-17 |isbn=978-0-85199-638-7 |via=[[Google Books]]}}</ref>  While the Rhamnaceae family contains many [[Nitrogen fixation|nitrogen-fixing]] species,<ref>{{cite web |title=Why Nitrogen Fixing Trees? (NFTA 89-03) |website=[[Winrock International]] Forestry and Natural Resource Management Program |publisher=Nitrogen Fixing Tree Association |date=September 1989 |url=https://winrock.org/factnet-a-lasting-impact/fact-sheets/ziziphus-mauritiana-a-valuable-tree-for-arid-and-semi-arid-lands/ |access-date=2023-02-28 |archive-date=2023-02-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230228093335/https://winrock.org/factnet-a-lasting-impact/fact-sheets/ziziphus-mauritiana-a-valuable-tree-for-arid-and-semi-arid-lands/ }}</ref> ''Z. mauritiana'' can form dense stands and become invasive in some areas, including [[Fiji]] and [[Australia]], where it has become a serious environmental weed.<ref name = "Chinee"/>

The species name ''mauritiana'' likely references the island of [[Mauritius]], despite the species not being native there, due to trade routes or the movement of plant specimens through the region during the 18th century when Mauritius was an important colonial hub. In taxonomy, newly described species were historically often associated with the nearest or most significant landmasses known at the time of discovery, rather than the exact location where the species was found.{{Citation needed|date=November 2025}}

''Ziziphus mauritiana'' has a rapidly developing taproot, a necessary adaptation to drought conditions. The species varies widely in height, from a bushy shrub {{convert|1.5|-|2|m|ft}} tall, to a tree {{convert|10|-|12|m|ft}} tall with a trunk diameter of about {{convert|30|cm|in}}. ''Z. mauritiana'' may be erect or wide-spreading, with gracefully drooping thorny branches and zigzag branchlets, with short, sharp straight or hooked thorns; some varieties are thornless.<ref name="GISD">{{cite web |title=Ziziphus mauritiana |work=[[Global Invasive Species Database]] |publisher=[[International Union for Conservation of Nature]] |url=https://www.iucngisd.org/gisd/species.php?sc=214 |access-date=2023-02-27}}</ref>

The leaves are alternate and ovate or oblong-elliptic in shape with rounded apices, with three main longitudinal veins originating from the [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]]. The size of the leaves ranges from {{convert|2.5|-|6.3|cm|in}} long and {{convert|2|-|4|cm|in}} wide. The upperside (adaxial surface) of the leaves is dark-green and smooth, while the underside (abaxial surface) is covered with hairs.<ref name="Dubey2024">{{cite journal |last1=Dubey |first1=Mahesh C. |last2=Mohanta |first2=Dambarudhar |title=Coexisting superhydrophobicity and superadhesion features of Ziziphus mauritiana abaxial leaf surface with possibility of biomimicking using electrospun microfibers |journal=Physics of Fluids |date=2024 |volume=36 |issue=1 |publisher=AIP Publishing |doi=10.1063/5.0181554}}</ref>

The flowers are tiny and yellow with five petals, located on leaf axils. They open fully in the early morning or later in the day, depending on the cultivar. Fertilisation relies on cross-pollination by insects attracted by the odour and nectar. Pollination is done by [[Honey bee|honeybees]], wasps (''[[Polistes]]'' sp.) and [[Housefly|houseflies]].<ref name="AFTD"/> Due to the [[protandrous]] nature of the flowers, the trees cannot reliably self-pollinate. The unpleasant scent of the flowers is caused by [[skatole]], a volatile organic compound released at high concentrations at [[anthesis]].

[[File:Ziziphus mauritiana fruit.jpg|thumb|Fruits at various stages of ripeness, with cracked pit showing the two seeds]]
This fast-growing tree bears fruit within three years. The [[fruit]] is an oval, obovate, round or oblong [[drupe]] that measures {{convert|2.5|cm|in}} diameter, though in some [[Cultivar|cultivars]] it can measure up to {{convert|6|cm|in}} long and {{convert|4|cm|in}} wide. When unripe, the skin is light green in colour while the flesh is white and crispy, with a bland, sour or slightly sweet flavour. The ripe fruit has a pleasant aroma and a soft, juicy and somewhat mealy texture, with wrinkled skin and a sweet-sour taste. Overripe fruits are more wrinkled, and the flesh becomes  soft, spongy and buff-coloured with a musky scent. Each fruit contains an oval or oblate rough pit, containing one or two ellipsoid red-brown kernels, each measuring {{convert|6|mm|in}} long.<ref>Indian jujube a potential fruit tree to improve the livelihood (2023) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10440574/</ref>

==Ecology==
This hardy tree can withstand extreme temperatures and thrives in rather dry or water-logged conditions with an annual rainfall of {{convert|125|-|2225|mm|in}}. In [[Fiji]], naturalised trees grow along roadsides and on agricultural land, usually near sea level but occasionally up to an elevation of {{convert|600|m|ft}}. It also grows well on laterite soils with good drainage, or sandy, gravelly, alluvial soil of dry riverbeds. In [[Australia]], this species grows on a wide variety of soil types, including cracking clays, solodic soils and deep alluvials, in tropical and subtropical areas with an average annual rainfall of {{convert|470|-|1200|mm|in}}. In the drier parts of this range, it grows best in [[riparian]] zones.<ref name="GISD"/><ref>The Biology of Australian Weeds
39. Ziziphus mauritiana Lam. (2002) https://caws.org.nz/PPQ1617/PPQ%2017-1%20pp002-11%20Grice.pdf</ref> Commercial cultivation usually extends up to {{convert|1000|m|ft}}. Above this elevation, the trees do not grow well, and cultivation becomes less economical.<ref name="AFTD">{{citation |first1=Caleb |last1=Orwa |first2=Anthony |last2=Mutua |first3=Roeland |last3=Kindt |first4=Ramni |last4=Jamnadass |first5=Anthony |last5=Simons |title=Ziziphus mauritiana {{!}} The AgroforesTree Database: a tree reference and selection guide |edition=version 4.0 |publisher=[[World Agroforestry Centre]] |date=2009 |url=https://apps.worldagroforestry.org/treedb2/AFTPDFS/Ziziphus_mauritiana.PDF |access-date=2023-02-28}}</ref>

While this species can withstand extreme conditions, it is more widespread in areas with an annual rainfall of {{convert|300|-|500|mm|in}}. In [[China]] and [[India]], it grows wild up to an elevation of {{convert|1650|m|ft}}. The minimum temperature for survival is {{convert|7|C|F}} and the maximum is {{convert|50|C|F}}. Studies report that this species flourishes in alkaline soils with a pH as high as 9.2. However, deep sandy loam to loamy soils with neutral or slightly alkaline pH are considered optimum for growth.<ref>{{cite web |title=Ziziphus mauritiana – A Valuable Tree for Arid and Semi-arid Lands (FACT Sheet 98-03) |website=[[Winrock International]] Forestry and Natural Resource Management Program |publisher=Forest, Farm, and Community Tree Network |date=July 1998 |url=https://winrock.org/factnet-a-lasting-impact/fact-sheets/ziziphus-mauritiana-a-valuable-tree-for-arid-and-semi-arid-lands/ |access-date=2009-07-17 |archive-date=2020-11-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201124121206/https://winrock.org/factnet-a-lasting-impact/fact-sheets/ziziphus-mauritiana-a-valuable-tree-for-arid-and-semi-arid-lands/ }}</ref>{{additional citations needed|date=September 2025}}

==Propagation==
Propagation is best done by seed, [[grafting]] or [[Cutting (plant)|cuttings]]. The seeds are spread by birds, livestock, feral pigs, humans and other mammals. Seeds may remain viable for over two years, but the germination rate decreases with age.<ref name="HORT"/> Cross-incompatibility occurs, and [[cultivar]]s have to be matched for good fruit set; some cultivars produce good crops parthenocarpically.{{Citation needed|date=June 2021}}

In India, there are 90 or more cultivars varying in growth habit, leaf shape, fruiting season, and fruit form, size, colour, flavour and storage quality. Among the important cultivars, 11 are described in the encyclopaedic ''Wealth of India'': ''Banarasi'' (or ''Banarsi'') ''Pewandi'', ''Dandan'', ''Kaithli'' (''Patham''), ''Muria Mahrara'', ''Narikelee'', ''Nazuk'', ''Sanauri 1'', ''Sanauri 5'', ''Thornless'' and ''Umran'' (''Umri''). Most of the cultivars have smooth and greenish-yellow to yellow skin.<ref name="HORT"/>

Seeds still in their pits need to be stored for 21–28 days to allow [[Seed_dormancy#Physiological_dormancy|after-ripening]] before planting. To stimulate faster germination, pits are placed in a 17–18% salt solution and all that float are discarded. The pits that sink are dipped in 500 [[Parts per million|ppm]] [[thiourea]] for four hours and then cracked, and the separated seeds can germinate in seven days.<ref name = "HORT"/>

Seedlings respond poorly to transplanting, so the seeds are best sown directly in the ground. Seedlings grown from wild seeds can be converted into improved [[Cultivar|cultivars]] by top-working and [[grafting]]. Nurseries are used for large-scale seedling and graft production. The seedlings grow best in full sunlight, and need to grow for as long as 15 months in the nursery before planting in the field.<ref name="AFTD"/>

Scientists in India have standardised propagation techniques for plant establishment. Budding is the easiest method to [[Vegetative reproduction|vegetatively propagate]] improved [[Cultivar|cultivars]]. with ring-budding and shield-budding being the most successful methods. Wild species are usually used as [[rootstock]], the most common being ''Z. rotundifolia'' in India and ''Z. spina-christi'' in Africa.<ref name="HORT"/>

==Cultivation and Uses==
''Ziziphus mauritiana'' is widely grown in both its native and introduced ranges, mainly for its fruit. The main producing regions of ''Z. mauritiana'' fruit are the arid and semi arid areas of [[India]]. The crop is also grown in [[Pakistan]], [[Bangladesh]], [[Vietnam]], the [[Caribbean]] and parts of [[Africa]]. From 1984 to 1995, with improved [[Cultivar|cultivars]], 0.9 million tonnes of fruit were produced on a land area of {{convert|88,000|ha|acre}}.  A tree in northern India can yield {{convert|80|-|200|kg|lb}} of fresh fruit per year in its prime bearing age of 10–20 years.<ref name="jules"/> 

[[File:TaoTa ZiziphusMauritiana.JPG|thumb|Unripe fruit in Vietnam, cut to show the pit in the middle]]
The fruit is eaten raw, used in beverages or made into preserves. It is rich in [[vitamin C]], second only to [[guava]], and much higher than citrus fruits and apples.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bâ |first1=A.M. |last2=Guissou |first2=T. |last3=Thioye |first3=B. |last4=Duponnois |first4=R. |last5=Fall |first5=F. |last6=Sylla |first6=S.N. |date=September 2023 |title=Arbuscular mycorrhizal symbiosis is a key factor to domesticate ''Ziziphus mauritiana'' Lam. in orchards |journal=South African Journal of Botany |volume=160 |pages=166–179 |doi=10.1016/j.sajb.2023.06.047 |bibcode=2023SAJB..160..166B |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Abdel-Sattar |first1=Mahmoud |last2=Almutairi |first2=Khalid F. |last3=Al-Saif |first3=Adel M. |last4=Ahmed |first4=Khaled A. |date=June 2021 |title=Fruit properties during the harvest period of eleven Indian jujube (Ziziphus mauritiana Lamk.) cultivars |journal=Saudi Journal of Biological Sciences |volume=28 |issue=6 |pages=3424–3432 |doi=10.1016/j.sjbs.2021.03.006 |pmid=34121881 |pmc=8176135 |bibcode=2021SJBS...28.3424A }}</ref> The unripe fruit is eaten much like an apple, sometimes with a little salt. In India, the ripe fruits are consumed raw or cooked, while slightly underripe fruits are candied. Ripe fruits can be made into a drink, or preserved by sun-drying and ground into powder.

The leaves are used to make an infusion in [[Indonesia]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Daun Bidara, Ini Manfaat dan Cara Mengonsumsinya |url=https://www.alodokter.com/daun-bidara-kenali-kandungan-dan-ragam-manfaatnya-untuk-kesehatan |website=alodokter.com |date=8 October 2023 |language=Indonesian |location=Indonesia |publisher=Kementerian Kesehatan Republik Indonesia |access-date=2025-11-20}}</ref> In [[Venezuela]], fruits are made into a [[liqueur]] called ''crema de ponsigue''. Seed kernels are eaten in times of famine. The leaves are also eaten by camels, cattle and goats.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Heuzé |first1=V |last2=Tran |first2=G |last3=Boval |first3=M |last4=Lebas |first4=F |year=2017 |title=Indian jujube (Ziziphus mauritiana) |work=Feedipedia, a programme by INRA, CIRAD, AFZ and FAO |url= https://www.feedipedia.org/node/80}}</ref><ref name = "HORT"/>

In India and [[Queensland|Queensland, Australia]], the flowers are a source of nectar for honeybees. The honey is golden amber in colour with a malty, earthy flavour.

The timber is hard, strong, fine-grained, fine-textured, durable and reddish in colour, used in a wide variety of applications including boat ribs, agricultural tools and footwear.<ref name = "HORT"/> The wood is also used as fuel in many areas. In tropical Africa, the flexible branches are wrapped as retaining bands around conical thatched roofs of huts, and are twined together to form thorny corral walls to retain livestock.

[[File:Zizyphus mauritiana bark.jpg|250px|thumb|upright|Bark]]

Traditional remedies using ''Z. mauritiana'' address a wide range of ailments, particularly in India where the plant is commonly known as ''ber''. To treat rheumatism, a [[poultice]] made from leaves, roots and ''[[Senna auriculata]]'' roots is applied to the affected area. Chronic coughs are treated with bark paste fried in [[ghee]] and taken with a small amount of rock salt, while vomiting is treated by consuming root-bark powder mixed with rice-washing water. Leaf juice is gently applied around the eyes for eye disorders and is also used in hair care, where a paste of ''ber'', amla (''[[Phyllanthus emblica]]'') and neem (''[[Azadirachta indica]]'') leaves is applied to the scalp. For wounds, pimples, acne, abscesses, boils and carbuncles, a poultice of leaves is applied topically. Indigestion is treated by taking root paste orally, while dried leaf powder is traditionally used to manage [[diabetes]]. A decoction of the leaves is used as a hair wash, in addition to a diuretic to manage fluid retention, [[oedema]], [[sciatica]], [[kidney stones]], lymphatic swelling, [[glaucoma]] and liver disorders. For diarrhoea, powdered dried fruit is taken with water, and for dysentery, leaf juices from ''[[Kalanchoe pinnata|patharchatta]]'', ''[[Syzygium cumini|jamun]]'' and ''ber'' are taken together.<ref name = "HORT"/><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Prakash |first1=Om |last2=Usmani |first2=Shazia |last3=Singh |first3=Ruchi |last4=Singh |first4=Namrata |last5=Gupta |first5=Amresh |last6=Ved |first6=Akash |title=A panoramic view on phytochemical, nutritional, and therapeutic attributes of Ziziphus mauritiana Lam.: A comprehensive review |journal=Phytotherapy Research |date=January 2021 |volume=35 |issue=1 |pages=63–77 |doi=10.1002/ptr.6769 |pmid=32633009 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Alsayari |first1=Abdulrhman |last2=Wahab |first2=Shadma |title=Genus Ziziphus for the treatment of chronic inflammatory diseases |journal=Saudi Journal of Biological Sciences |date=December 2021 |volume=28 |issue=12 |pages=6897–6914 |doi=10.1016/j.sjbs.2021.07.076 |pmid=34866990 |pmc=8626254 |bibcode=2021SJBS...28.6897A }}</ref>

In [[West Bengal]], it is offered to [[Saraswati|Goddess Saraswati]] and people refrain from consuming the fruit before offering it to the goddess.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Basant Panchami 2022: Why Do Bengalis Refrain From Eating Ber (Jujube) Fruit Before Saraswati Puja |url=https://food.ndtv.com/food-drinks/basant-panchami-2018-why-do-bengalis-refrain-from-eating-ber-jujube-fruit-before-saraswati-puja-1801717 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250316051942/https://food.ndtv.com/food-drinks/basant-panchami-2018-why-do-bengalis-refrain-from-eating-ber-jujube-fruit-before-saraswati-puja-1801717 |archive-date=2025-03-16 |access-date= |work=NDTV Food |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Season and Harvesting==
[[File:Ziziphus mauritiana (fruits sale).jpg|thumb|Ripe and unripe jujube fruits for sale at the Luangwa Bridge in [[Zambia]]]]
Plants are capable of seed production once they reach a height of about {{convert|1|m|ft}}. Wild-growing plants in northern Australia may take eight years to reach this size. A tree can produce 5,000–10,000 fruits a year if grown directly from seed, or up to 30,000 fruits if grafted.<ref name = "HORT"/>

In India, certain cultivars ripen as early as October, while others mature from mid-February to mid-March, in March, or from mid-March through April. In the [[Asyut Governorate]] of [[Egypt]], the tree bears fruit twice a year—the main crop in early spring and a second in autumn. Indian orchards typically require two or three hand-pickings from ladders, with a worker able to harvest about {{convert|50|kg|lb}} per day. Remaining fruits are shaken from the branches. After being wrapped in white cloth, the fruits are packed into paper-lined burlap sacks for transport to markets across the country.<ref name = "HORT"/><ref>{{cite web |title=Seed Leaflet No. 85 {{!}} ''Ziziphus mauritiana'' Lam. |first=Dorthe |last=Jøker |date=October 2003 |publisher=[[Danish International Development Agency]] Forest Seed Centre |url=https://www.doc-developpement-durable.org/file/Culture/Arbres-Fruitiers/FICHES_ARBRES/jujubier/ziziphus_mauritiana_85.pdf |access-date=2009-07-17}}</ref>

== Pests and Diseases ==
{{More citations needed section|date=June 2021}}
{{Multiple image
| image1            = Fruit fly infested ber fruit.jpg
| image2            = Adult of ber fruit fly.jpg
| align             = left
| caption1          = Fruit fly-infested fruit
| caption2          = Adult fruit fly on a leaf
}}
Fruit flies are the biggest threat to ''Z. mauritiana'' fruits. Some [[cultivar|cultivars]] are more susceptible than others—the flies prefer the largest, sweetest fruits, while a nearby tree bearing smaller, less-sweet fruits suffers little damage. Full-grown larvae exit the fruit by making holes in the skin, and then drop to the ground to form pupae. Control is possible by destroying the pupae with irrigation during summer or subjecting the soil to heat by burning grass, as well as regular application of insecticide.<ref name = "HORT"/>

Caterpillars, especially [[Limacodidae|slug moth]] larvae attack the foliage. [[Mite]]s form scale-like galls on twigs, limiting growth and reducing fruit production. Lesser pests include the larvae of ''[[Meridarchis scyrodes]]'', which bores into the fruit.

The tree is susceptible to infestation by the parasitic [[dodder]] ''[[Cuscuta reflexa]]'', which causes considerable damage by extracting nutrients from its host and smothering it.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Das |first1=Debarata |title=Host Diversity of ''Cuscuta reflexa'' Roxb. in Darjeeling District, West Bengal, India |journal=International Journal for Science and Advance Research in Technology |date=June 2018 |volume=4 |issue=6 |pages=2395–1052 |url=https://ijsart.com/public/storage/paper/pdf/IJSARTV4I624251.pdf }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Khan |first1=Mirza Hakim |title=The Destructive Role of Cuscuta as a Parasite |journal= Pakistan Journal of Forestry |date=2002 |volume=52 |issue=2 |pages=127–129 |url=https://www.pfi.gov.pk/control_panel/pdf/06._The_destructive_role_of_Cuscuta_as_a_parasite.pdf |access-date=2025-11-20}}</ref> Powdery mildew causes defoliation and fruit-drop, but it can be adequately controlled.<ref name = "AFTD"/> Lesser diseases are [[Sooty mold|sooty mould]], [[Wood-decay fungus|brown rot]] and [[leaf spot]]. Leaf spot results from infestation by ''[[Cercospora]]'' spp. and ''[[Isariopsis|Isariopsis indica]]'' var. ''zizyphi''. In 1973, a [[Witch's broom|witches'-broom disease]] caused by a [[mycoplasma]]-like organism was found in ''ber'' plants near [[Savitribai Phule Pune University|Poona University]]. Grafting or budding diseased scions onto healthy ''Z. mauritiana'' seedlings was found to be the cause of transmission. Leaf rust, caused by ''[[Phakopsora|Phakopsora zizyphivulgaris]]'', ranges from mild to severe on all commercial cultivars in [[Punjab]].

In storage, the fruits are susceptible to fungal attack by several species, including ''[[Fusarium]]'' spp., ''[[Nigrospora oryzae]]'', ''[[Epicoccum nigrum]]'' and ''[[Glomerella cingulata]]''.
